blocks.title: Race Overview
blocks.content: Val d'Aran 160K was designed to test every aspect of mountain ultrarunning. The course combines long sustained climbs, highly technical descents, runnable valleys and repeated transitions between terrain types, forcing athletes to constantly adapt their pacing strategy. Unlike races where one decisive climb determines the outcome, Val d'Aran rewards runners capable of repeating quality efforts over an entire day in the mountains.

The opening 25 kilometres immediately established the first selection. Two demanding climbs placed a premium on climbing efficiency rather than outright speed, creating the initial gaps that would shape the remainder of the race. While many athletes attempted to remain in contention, only a small group demonstrated the ability to sustain competitive VPI values without accumulating excessive fatigue. Already by the third checkpoint, the leading contenders had separated themselves from the rest of the field, illustrating how early climbing efficiency can define the tactical landscape of an ultra-distance mountain race.

The middle section represented the true heart of the competition. Successive climbs exceeding 800 and 1,300 metres of elevation gain progressively transformed small time differences into meaningful tactical advantages. Importantly, the race did not feature a single catastrophic collapse among the front runners. Instead, positions evolved through gradual performance degradation. Athletes capable of preserving climbing efficiency maintained their positions, while those whose VPI declined were unable to recover despite respectable descending performances. This progressive separation is one of the clearest signatures of Val d'Aran's demanding profile.

From a broader perspective, the race highlighted one of the defining characteristics of Val d'Aran 160K: this is a course where consistency consistently outperforms explosiveness. The decisive differences emerged not because one athlete produced extraordinary individual segments, but because the eventual winners repeatedly maintained high performance while their competitors gradually lost efficiency. The data confirms that sustainable climbing ability, controlled descending, and intelligent effort distribution remain the three pillars of success on one of Europe's most demanding mountain ultras.

Gabriel Santos Rueda (5) delivered one of the most complete performances, controlling the race through consistency rather than explosive attacks. Although he never dominated every checkpoint, he remained among the fastest athletes from the opening climb to the finish, steadily converting small advantages into a decisive victory. His race perfectly reflects the demands of Val d'Aran 160K: success came not from isolated moments of brilliance, but from sustaining elite performance over more than twenty-one hours of continuous mountain running.

The Vertical Trail Labs metrics reinforce that conclusion. Rueda (5) was not only one of the strongest climbers, but also one of the most efficient descenders throughout the race. His Vertical Performance Index (VPI) consistently ranked among the highest of the Top 10, while his Descending Management Index (DMI) remained equally competitive. Very few athletes managed to combine both qualities simultaneously. Rather than excelling on a single terrain, Rueda continuously arrived at each climb with enough strength to repeat another elite ascent while protecting his legs on every descent.

Behind him, Théo Soriano (27) and Delbi Villa Gongora (22) produced equally intelligent races. Neither attempted risky tactical moves or dramatic accelerations. Instead, both built their podium finishes through disciplined pacing and remarkably stable efficiency. Their checkpoint evolution shows very limited fluctuations compared with other contenders, demonstrating excellent race management across every terrain type. As fatigue accumulated, both athletes continued to perform at a consistently high level while others gradually lost climbing efficiency.

One of the clearest characteristics of the men's race is how early the podium positions began to consolidate. During the opening mountain sectors several runners exchanged positions, but after halfway the leaderboard became increasingly stable. From that point onward, significant gains generally resulted from another athlete slowing down rather than from direct attacks. On a course featuring more than 11,400 metres of climbing, accumulated fatigue became the dominant performance factor, rewarding athletes capable of maintaining efficiency rather than producing occasional fast splits.

The position evolution chart also highlights two of the most remarkable stories of resilience. Josu Azkune Cordon (83) dropped as low as 52nd place during the opening mountain block before producing one of the strongest recoveries of the race, climbing steadily through the field to reach the Top 15 by mid-race and ultimately finishing tenth overall. Equally impressive was Jean-Marie Diverrez (29), who fell dramatically to 55th position around kilometre 33, only to recover progressively throughout the second quarter of the race and return to the Top 15 by kilometre 82 before securing eighth place at the finish. These performances underline how patience and intelligent pacing often outweigh early positioning in ultra-distance racing.

Perhaps the greatest lesson from the men's competition is that Val d'Aran rewards complete mountain runners rather than specialists. Athletes capable of climbing exceptionally well but descending inefficiently gradually lost contact with the leaders, while aggressive descenders were unable to compensate for time lost on the sustained climbs. The final podium belonged to the three runners who best combined climbing power, descending control and endurance durability. Their performances demonstrate that the decisive performance indicator was not maximum speed on any individual sector, but the ability to reproduce high-level efficiency over every climb and descent across 160 kilometres.

Katarzyna Dombrowska (4) controlled the women's race with remarkable authority, establishing herself among the leaders from the opening climb and never relinquishing that position. Rather than relying on spectacular attacks, she gradually expanded her advantage through relentless consistency across every mountain sector. Her victory was built on disciplined pacing, efficient climbing and excellent terrain management, allowing her to maintain a stable performance profile for more than thirty-three hours of racing.

The performance metrics reveal why her race proved so difficult to challenge. Dombrowska (4) consistently ranked among the strongest athletes in both VPI and DMI, demonstrating that her superiority extended beyond climbing alone. While many competitors excelled either uphill or downhill, she remained highly efficient in both disciplines throughout the race. This balanced performance minimized physiological stress, reduced cumulative muscular damage and enabled her to preserve climbing strength deep into the final mountain sectors.

Behind the winner, Aroa Sio (6) delivered a highly disciplined race to secure second place. Although she never seriously threatened Dombrowska's lead, she avoided major fluctuations and maintained competitive climbing efficiency throughout the event. Salomé Grihon (298) completed the podium after another impressively controlled performance, remaining close to the leading positions while successfully managing fatigue over one of the most demanding courses on the UTMB calendar. Like the men's podium, the three leading women displayed remarkably similar pacing strategies centred on consistency rather than aggression.
VPI Progression

Unlike the men's race, the women's competition featured greater movement throughout the Top 10 during the opening stages. Several athletes exchanged positions repeatedly as they adapted their pace to the demands of the course. However, once the race entered its second half, those position changes became progressively less frequent. As cumulative fatigue increased, opportunities for recovery diminished and the athletes with the strongest endurance profiles gradually separated themselves from the rest of the field.

Another defining characteristic of the women's race was how efficiently the podium athletes managed the transition between prolonged climbs and technical descents. Despite the demanding terrain, none relied on excessive downhill risk to gain time. Instead, they consistently protected their legs before each subsequent climb, allowing them to sustain higher climbing efficiency later in the race. This conservative descending strategy ultimately proved more effective than pursuing short-term gains at the expense of long-term performance.

Ultimately, the women's race reinforces exactly the same conclusion as the men's competition. Val d'Aran 160K rewarded athletes capable of maintaining stable physiological efficiency rather than producing isolated moments of exceptional speed. Katarzyna Dombrowska's (4) victory illustrates that perfectly. She was rarely spectacular on any single checkpoint, yet she was consistently excellent across every terrain type. Combined with intelligent pacing, efficient descending and durable climbing performance, that consistency transformed small advantages into a commanding victory on one of Europe's toughest mountain ultras.

blocks.title: Final Insight
blocks.content:
Perhaps the defining characteristic of the 2026 Val d'Aran 160K was not simply its 11,441 metres of elevation gain, but how much of the race unfolded above 1,800 metres of altitude. 

Competitors spent 74.3 km (46% of the entire course) above 1,800 metres, making prolonged altitude exposure one of the race's defining physiological challenges. At those elevations, reduced oxygen availability amplifies the cost of every climb, accelerates fatigue and places even greater importance on efficient pacing and nutrition.

The Performance Indexes reinforce this picture. The strongest athletes were not those producing the highest isolated VPI or DMI values, but those capable of maintaining both metrics throughout the race. Gabriel Santos Rueda (5) and Katarzyna Dombrowska (4) consistently ranked among the leaders in both climbing and descending efficiency, demonstrating that success at Val d'Aran required complete mountain-running proficiency rather than excellence in a single discipline. Their ability to repeatedly transition from demanding climbs to technical descents without significant efficiency loss ultimately separated them from the rest of the field.


Finally, the position evolution charts remind us that a 160-kilometre ultra is rarely won during the opening hours. Exceptional recoveries from athletes such as Josu Azkune Cordon (83) and Jean-Marie Diverrez (29) demonstrate that patience often outperforms early aggression. 

At Val d'Aran, resilience, terrain management and durable efficiency mattered far more than early checkpoint rankings. That is precisely what the Vertical Trail Labs metrics are designed to measure: not who was fastest at any single moment, but who sustained elite performance across an entire mountain ultra.
